title: Αἴλουρος καὶ ἀλεκτρυών
part: The Cat and the Cock (Chambry 12 · Perry 16)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 12 (= Perry 16). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Αἴλουρος, συλλαβὼν ἀλεκτρυόνα, μετ’ εὐλόγου τοῦτον αἰτίας ἠβουλήθη καταφαγεῖν.
sentences.tr: Ailouros, syllabōn alektryona, met’ eulogou touton aitias ēboulēthē kataphagein.
sentences.l: A cat, having seized a cock, wished to devour him with a plausible charge.
sentences.i: A cat caught a cock and wanted to eat him — but with a decent-looking case for it.
sentences.n: μετ’ εὐλόγου … αἰτίας is one phrase split around τοῦτον: hyperbaton, where an adjective is parted from its noun by other words. Read forward to the noun and the phrase closes up. εὔλογος is “plausible, specious” — sounding reasonable, not being right, which is the whole point of what follows. αἰτία is both “cause” and “accusation”; here it is the charge the cat intends to bring, and the fable that follows is a mock trial, prosecution speech and defence and all.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ κατηγόρει αὐτοῦ ὡς ὀχληρὸς εἴη τοῖς ἀνθρώποις νύκτωρ κεκραγὼς καὶ μὴ συγχωρῶν ὕπνου τυγχάνειν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē katēgorei autou hōs ochlēros eiē tois anthrōpois nyktōr kekragōs kai mē synchōrōn hypnou tynchanein.
sentences.l: And indeed he accused him, that he was troublesome to men, crowing by night and not allowing them to obtain sleep.
sentences.i: And so he charged him with being a nuisance to men, screeching in the night and not letting them get any sleep.
sentences.n: ὡς with the optative (εἴη) after a past verb of saying: the charge is reported, not vouched for by the narrator — the regular shift out of the indicative when the main verb is past. κεκραγώς is a perfect participle with present force; κράζω “shriek” makes its perfect mean “is in full cry”. τυγχάνω takes the genitive of what one obtains (ὕπνου). κατηγορέω, the courtroom word for prosecuting, also takes the genitive of the accused.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δ’ ἀπολογουμένου ἐπὶ τῇ ἐκείνων ὠφελείᾳ τοῦτο ποιεῖν, ὡς ἐπὶ τὰ συνήθη τῶν ἔργων ἐγείρεσθαι, πάλιν ὁ αἴλουρος αἰτίαν ἐπέφερεν ὡς ἀσεβὴς εἴη περὶ τὴν φύσιν, μητρὶ καὶ ἀδελφαῖς συμμιγνύμενος.
sentences.tr: Tou d’ apologoumenou epi tēi ekeinōn ōpheleiāi touto poiein, hōs epi ta synēthē tōn ergōn egeiresthai, palin ho ailouros aitian epepheren hōs asebēs eiē peri tēn physin, mētri kai adelphais symmignymenos.
sentences.l: And he defending himself, that he did this for their benefit, so as to be roused to their accustomed tasks, again the cat brought a charge, that he was impious as regards nature, coupling with his mother and his sisters.
sentences.i: When the cock pleaded that he did it for their own good, so that they might wake to their usual work, the cat brought a second charge: that he was an offender against nature, coupling with his mother and his sisters.
sentences.n: Τοῦ δ’ ἀπολογουμένου is a genitive absolute — a noun and participle set in the genitive outside the sentence's grammar to supply the attendant circumstance — and it carries an infinitive (ποιεῖν) for the content of what he pleads. ὡς with an infinitive (ἐγείρεσθαι) gives purpose or intended result. ἀσεβής is a religious and legal word: ἀσέβεια was an indictable offence at Athens, so the cat is still speaking as a prosecutor.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς ὠφέλειαν τῶν δεσποτῶν πράττειν φήσαντος, πολλῶν αὐτοῖς ἐντεῦθεν ὠῶν τικτομένων, ὁ αἴλουρος εἰπών· « Ἀλλ’ εἰ σύ γε πολλῶν εὐπορεῖς εὐπροσώπων ἀπολογιῶν, ἔγωγε μέντοι ἄτροφος οὐ μενῶ », τοῦτον κατεθοινήσατο.
sentences.tr: Tou de kai touto pros ōpheleian tōn despotōn prattein phēsantos, pollōn autois enteuthen ōōn tiktomenōn, ho ailouros eipōn: « All’ ei sy ge pollōn euporeis euprosōpōn apologiōn, egōge mentoi atrophos ou menō », touton katethoinēsato.
sentences.l: And he having said that he did this too for the benefit of his masters, many eggs being laid for them from it, the cat, having said: « But if you at any rate are well supplied with plausible defences, I for my part shall not stay unfed », made a banquet of him.
sentences.i: When the cock said that this too was for his owners' good, since it got them plenty of eggs, the cat said, « You may have no shortage of respectable-looking defences; I, for my part, do not intend to go unfed », and made a meal of him.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes in a row (Τοῦ … φήσαντος, then πολλῶν … τικτομένων giving the reason). εὐπρόσωπος is literally “fair-faced” — an argument that looks respectable from the front. κατεθοινήσατο is built on θοίνη, “a feast”: not merely ate, but banqueted on him. The raised dot · is the Greek colon; the guillemets « » are Chambry's editorial quotation marks, kept as printed.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι ἡ πονηρὰ φύσις πλημμελεῖν αἱρουμένη, εἰ μὴ μετ’ εὐλόγου δυνηθείη προσχήματος, ἀπαρακαλύπτως γε μὴν πονηρεύεται.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti hē ponēra physis plēmmelein hairoumenē, ei mē met’ eulogou dynētheiē proschēmatos, aparakalyptōs ge mēn ponēreuetai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that a wicked nature, choosing to do wrong, if it should not be able to do so under a plausible screen, does its wickedness undisguised all the same.
sentences.i: The fable shows that a bad nature bent on wrongdoing, if it cannot manage the thing under a decent pretext, will do it barefaced instead.
sentences.n: εἰ μή with the optative (δυνηθείη) supposes a case rather than reporting one: “should it not be able”. πρόσχημα is what is held out in front — a screen, a pretext; ἀπαρακαλύπτως is its exact opposite, “with nothing drawn over it”. γε μήν concedes and then insists: “all the same”. Note μετ’ εὐλόγου … προσχήματος split around the verb, the same hyperbaton the fable opened with.
